title: What causes memory leaks in Java despite GC (static collections, unclosed resources, ThreadLocal in pools, unremoved listeners, unbounded caches, inner class holding outer reference), and how do you diagnose one end-to-end (jstat → GC log → heap dump → MAT leak suspects → reference chain)?
shortTitle: What causes memory leaks in Java despite GC, and how do you diagnose one end-to-end?

s1_definition.profdef: A Java memory leak is a logical leak: objects are no longer needed but remain reachable through a live reference chain, so the garbage collector, which only frees unreachable objects, can never reclaim them. Common causes are static collections that grow without bound, unclosed resources, `ThreadLocal` values retained by pooled threads, listeners or callbacks that are registered but never removed, unbounded caches, and non-static inner classes holding an implicit reference to their outer instance. End-to-end diagnosis typically follows jstat to watch GC and the live set, GC logs to confirm old-generation growth, a heap dump, MAT's leak suspects report, and finally the dominator tree and reference chain back to the GC root that keeps the memory alive.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India's vault where old files should be shredded once a case closes, but a clerk keeps a master index that still lists every closed case, so the shredding crew (the garbage collector) is not allowed to destroy any of them because the index still points to them. The files are useless but still referenced, so the vault fills up. Diagnosing it is like a forensic audit: first you watch the vault filling faster than it empties, then you take a full inventory snapshot, then a tool highlights the suspiciously huge index, and finally you trace the chain from the index all the way back to the clerk who refuses to let go.
s1_definition.oneliner: A Java leak is live but unneeded references the GC cannot free, and you diagnose it by watching GC growth, taking a heap dump, and tracing the reference chain from the bloated objects back to the GC root.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Java memory leak is a logical leak: objects are no longer needed but remain reachable through a live reference chain, so the garbage collector, which only frees unreachable objects, can never reclaim them. Common causes are static collections that grow without bound, unclosed resources, `ThreadLocal` values retained by pooled threads, listeners or callbacks that are registered but never removed, unbounded caches, and non-static inner classes holding an implicit reference to their outer instance. End-to-end diagnosis typically follows jstat to watch GC and the live set, GC logs to confirm old-generation growth, a heap dump, MAT's leak suspects report, and finally the dominator tree and reference chain back to the GC root that keeps the memory alive.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India's vault where old files should be shredded once a case closes, but a clerk keeps a master index that still lists every closed case, so the shredding crew (the garbage collector) is not allowed to destroy any of them because the index still points to them. The files are useless but still referenced, so the vault fills up. Diagnosing it is like a forensic audit: first you watch the vault filling faster than it empties, then you take a full inventory snapshot, then a tool highlights the suspiciously huge index, and finally you trace the chain from the index all the way back to the clerk who refuses to let go.

**One line to remember:** A Java leak is live but unneeded references the GC cannot free, and you diagnose it by watching GC growth, taking a heap dump, and tracing the reference chain from the bloated objects back to the GC root.

sections.s2_technical:
The garbage collector frees only objects that are unreachable from GC roots, so a leak in Java is never truly unreferenced memory; it is memory you forgot to stop referencing. Static collections are the classic culprit: a `static List` or `static Map` that you add to and never remove from lives for the whole application, so everything it holds is immortal. Unbounded caches are the same pattern with good intentions; without an eviction policy or size limit a cache grows until the heap is gone, which is why I always bound a cache with a size or TTL.

Unclosed resources leak because objects like streams, connections, and sessions hold native handles and often register themselves somewhere; failing to close them in a try-with-resources keeps them and their buffers alive. ThreadLocal leaks are subtle and dangerous in thread pools: a pooled thread never dies, so a value you set in a ThreadLocal and forget to remove stays attached to that long-lived thread forever, and in a web container this can also pin the whole web application classloader. The fix is to always remove the ThreadLocal in a finally block. Unremoved listeners and callbacks leak because registering a listener gives the publisher a strong reference to it; if you never deregister, the publisher keeps the listener, and often the object that owns it, alive for as long as the publisher lives. Non-static inner classes and lambdas capturing `this` hold an implicit reference to the enclosing instance, so a long-lived object holding such an inner instance keeps the whole outer object alive even if you only wanted the small inner piece.

The end-to-end diagnosis is a disciplined pipeline. First I use `jstat -gcutil <pid> 1s` to watch the old generation and the live set after full GCs; a leak shows the post-GC old-gen usage trending upward over time rather than returning to a baseline. Next I enable GC logging with `-Xlog:gc*` and confirm that full GCs reclaim less and less, which distinguishes a leak from a mere spike. Then I capture a heap dump, either with `jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap.hprof <pid>` or automatically via `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError`. I open it in Eclipse MAT and run the Leak Suspects report, which points at the biggest retained sets. The decisive step is the dominator tree and the "path to GC roots excluding weak references," which shows the exact reference chain keeping the objects alive, for example a static cache holding thousands of statement objects. A senior nuance: always compare two heap dumps taken minutes apart to see what is growing, use retained size rather than shallow size to find the real offender, and remember that weak and soft references, and tools that only look at live objects, change what you see; the whole point is to trace the chain back to the single GC root you can then remove.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's statement service keeps a static map of every statement it has ever generated, meaning to cache them, but it never evicts, so after a few days the heap climbs and full GCs free less each time. This is exactly the static-collection and unbounded-cache leak — live references the GC cannot reclaim.

Problem 2 — The same service runs on a thread pool and stashes the current user in a ThreadLocal but forgets to remove it, so each pooled thread permanently retains the last user it served. This is exactly the ThreadLocal-in-a-pool leak, which also pins everything that user object references.

The demo reproduces both leaks in a bounded, catchable way, shows the symptoms through a simple growth log, and walks the diagnosis pipeline in comments and commands. Classes and steps: `StatementCacheLeak` (static map leak), `UserContextLeak` (ThreadLocal leak), and `LeakDemo` plus the jstat and MAT command recipe.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
memory-leak-lab/
├── pom.xml
├── src/
│   └── main/
│       └── java/com/bank/leak/
│           ├── LeakDemo.java                 (runs both leaks + prints growth)
│           ├── StatementCacheLeak.java       (static unbounded cache)
│           └── UserContextLeak.java          (ThreadLocal not removed in a pool)
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run with GC logging and automatic heap dump on OOM
java -Xmx256m -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError \
  -XX:HeapDumpPath=/tmp -cp target/classes com.bank.leak.LeakDemo

# ── Diagnosis pipeline ──
# 1) Watch GC + live set: post-GC old-gen should NOT keep climbing
jstat -gcutil <pid> 1s

# 2) Confirm from GC log that full GCs reclaim less over time
grep "Pause Full" gc.log

# 3) Capture a live heap dump
jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap.hprof <pid>

# 4) Open heap.hprof in Eclipse MAT → run "Leak Suspects" report
# 5) Use the Dominator Tree + "Path to GC Roots (exclude weak)" to find the chain:
#      static STATEMENT_CACHE → HashMap$Node[] → byte[] (thousands)  ← the leak
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two thousand statement generations and four pooled requests for Rajesh and Priya.

Step 1 — The loop calls generateStatement two thousand times, each adding an eight-kilobyte blob to the static STATEMENT_CACHE map that is never evicted. Because the map is static and reachable from a GC root, every blob stays live, and the warning logs show the cache size only ever growing.

Step 2 — The demo submits four tasks to a fixed pool of four threads. Each task sets a 512-kilobyte user context into a ThreadLocal and returns without removing it. Since the pool reuses the same four threads, each thread now permanently retains its last user context.

Step 3 — To diagnose, jstat shows the post-full-GC old generation trending upward instead of returning to a baseline, and the GC log confirms full GCs are reclaiming less each time, which proves a leak rather than a transient spike.

Step 4 — A heap dump opened in MAT runs the Leak Suspects report, which flags the large retained set, and the dominator tree with the path to GC roots traces the chain from the static STATEMENT_CACHE map, and separately from the pooled threads' ThreadLocalMap, down to the thousands of retained byte arrays, pinpointing both the static-cache and ThreadLocal roots to fix.

```
2026-10-26 15:50:01 [WARNING] STATEMENT_CACHE size=500 (never evicted → leak ...)
2026-10-26 15:50:01 [WARNING] STATEMENT_CACHE size=2000 (never evicted → leak ...)
2026-10-26 15:50:01 [SEVERE] Leak 1 retained 2000 statements that GC can NEVER reclaim ...
2026-10-26 15:50:03 [SEVERE] Leak 2: each of the 4 pooled threads still holds a 512KB user context ...
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  CAUSE A — static unbounded cache
    generateStatement() ─► STATEMENT_CACHE.put(...)   (static, never removed)
      GC root: class StatementCacheLeak → static field → HashMap → byte[] ×2000
      GC cannot free: still reachable → LEAK

  CAUSE B — ThreadLocal in a pool
    pool thread ─► CURRENT_USER.set(512KB)  (no remove())
      GC root: Thread (pooled, immortal) → ThreadLocalMap → Entry.value (512KB)
      GC cannot free: thread never dies → LEAK

  DIAGNOSIS PIPELINE
    jstat -gcutil ──► old-gen climbs post-GC (not a spike)
       ▼
    -Xlog:gc* ──────► "Pause Full" reclaims less each time
       ▼
    jmap -dump ─────► heap.hprof
       ▼
    MAT Leak Suspects ─► biggest retained set highlighted
       ▼
    Dominator Tree + Path to GC Roots ─► static map / ThreadLocalMap → byte[]  (ROOT found)
```

```
  ═══ HLD — Leak Detection in Production ═══

  ┌──────────────┐  JMX/metrics  ┌──────────────┐  alert  ┌──────────────┐
  │ Banking App  │──────────────→│ Prometheus   │────────→│ PagerDuty    │

  └──────────────┘             │ Leak Suspects → Dominator    │
                               │ Tree → Path to GC Roots      │

```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Leak Causes → Fixes ═══

  ┌─ Causes and Fixes (as prose) ─────────────────────────────────┐
  │ static collection : add-only map       → bound size / clear     │
  │ unbounded cache   : no eviction        → Caffeine size + TTL    │
  │ unclosed resource : stream/conn open   → try-with-resources     │
  │ ThreadLocal pool  : set, never remove  → remove() in finally    │
  │ unremoved listener: register, no remove → deregister on dispose  │
  │ inner class ref   : captures outer this → static nested / weak   │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: cache holds data; lifecycle owner clears it — one job each   │
  │ O: swap HashMap for a bounded Caffeine cache, no call changes   │
  │ D: depend on a Cache interface, not a raw static map            │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Diagnosis Call Chain ──────────────────────────────────────
  1. jstat -gcutil <pid> 1s      → post-GC old-gen trending up
  2. -Xlog:gc* ; grep Pause Full → reclamation shrinking
  3. jmap -dump:live             → heap.hprof
  4. MAT Leak Suspects           → biggest retained set
  5. Dominator Tree + GC Roots   → reference chain to the root
  6. remove the root (bound/clear/remove/deregister)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The first thing I clarify is why leaks happen in a garbage-collected language at all. The collector only frees objects that are unreachable from GC roots, so a Java leak is never truly unreferenced memory; it is memory I forgot to stop referencing. The objects are useless but still reachable through a live chain, so the collector is not allowed to reclaim them. That reframing points straight at the common causes.

The classic cause is a static collection, a static list or map that I add to and never remove from, which lives for the whole application and makes everything it holds immortal; an unbounded cache is the same pattern with good intentions, which is why I always bound a cache with a size limit or a TTL. Unclosed resources leak because they hold native handles and buffers, so I use try-with-resources. ThreadLocal values are a subtle and dangerous one in thread pools, because a pooled thread never dies, so a value I set and forget to remove stays attached to that thread forever and can even pin a whole web application classloader, and the fix is to always remove it in a finally block. Unremoved listeners leak because registering gives the publisher a strong reference to the listener, so I must deregister on dispose. And a non-static inner class or a lambda capturing this holds an implicit reference to its enclosing instance, so a long-lived object holding it keeps the whole outer object alive.

My end-to-end diagnosis is a disciplined pipeline. I start with jstat to watch the old generation and the live set after full garbage collections; a real leak shows the post-GC usage trending upward instead of returning to a baseline. I enable GC logging to confirm that full collections reclaim less and less, which distinguishes a leak from a spike. Then I capture a heap dump, either with jmap or automatically on out-of-memory, and open it in Eclipse MAT. The Leak Suspects report points me at the biggest retained sets, and the decisive step is the dominator tree with the path to GC roots, which shows the exact reference chain keeping the objects alive.

In my banking work at National Bank of India the statement service leaked exactly this way: a static map cached every statement forever, and MAT's path to GC roots traced thousands of retained byte arrays straight back to that static field, which we fixed by switching to a bounded Caffeine cache. We also found a ThreadLocal user context that was never removed on a pooled thread, fixed with a remove in a finally block. The senior habit I always mention is to take two heap dumps a few minutes apart and compare them so I can see precisely what is growing, and to sort by retained size rather than shallow size so I find the real offender rather than a leaf object, because the whole goal is to trace the chain back to the single GC root I can then eliminate.
